items.abstract: <jats:p>Tool-augmented large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant promise as autonomous research agents, yet their reliability remains constrained by expensive verification mechanisms that require large judge models or human annotation. Current approaches to reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) depend on resource-intensive reward models, limiting their accessibility for researchers with computational constraints. We propose Consis-tencyVerify, a lightweight self-verification framework that leverages multi-sample consistency and uncertainty quantification to provide reliable reward signals for training tool-augmented agents. Our method eliminates the need for large external judge models by exploiting the inherent calibration properties of language models through temperature-scaled sampling and agreement-based scoring. We demonstrate that agents trained with ConsistencyVerify achieve competitive performance on information-seeking benchmarks while requiring only modest computational resources (single consumer GPU). Through extensive ablation studies on Natural Questions, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA, we show that consistency-based verification provides more stable training dynamics than traditional lexical metrics (F1, ROUGE) and approaches the performance of large judge-based RLAIF at a fraction of the computational cost. Our findings suggest that efficient self-verification through consistency modeling represents a viable path toward democratizing research agent development.</jats:p>
title: Efficient Self-Verification for Tool-Augmented Language Models via Consistency-Based Reward Modeling

items.abstract: <jats:p>Tool-augmented language model agents have emerged as a promising direction for deploying AI in real-world tasks, yet most evaluation studies focus on large proprietary models that are computationally expensive and inaccessible in resourceconstrained environments. This paper presents an empirical performance and cost&nbsp;evaluation of tool-augmented AI agents built on three open-source language models: llama-3.1-8b-instant (8B dense), meta-llama/llama-4-scout-17b-16e-instruct (17B active, 109B total MoE), and llama-3.3-70b-versatile (70B dense), accessed via the Groq inference API.</jats:p>
title: Tool-Augmented AI Agents on Small to Medium Language Models: A Performance and Cost Evaluation Study
Re-Initialization Token Learning for Tool-Augmented Large Language Models

items.abstract: <jats:p>Financial fraud detection systems must operate at national scale under strict constraints on latency, cost, explainability, and regulatory compliance. While Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate strong general reasoning capabilities, their deployment in real-time, regulated financial environments introduces challenges related to governance, auditability, and operational cost. This paper proposes a Small Language Model (SLM)-first architecture augmented with deterministic tool-based reasoning for scalable and compliant fraud detection. The system constrains generative reasoning through explicit evidence retrieval, structured tool invocation, and reproducible decision paths. We present a hybrid architecture in which SLMs handle highvolume structured decisions, while LLMs are selectively invoked for ambiguous edge cases. Through architectural formalization and simulated evaluation across multiple fraud typologies, we demonstrate improvements in latency, cost predictability, and audit traceability compared to LLM-centric approaches. The proposed framework aligns advanced AI reasoning with regulatory model governance requirements, enabling deployable intelligence in financial fraud operations.</jats:p>
title: Fighting Fraud Smarter: Small Language Models with Tool-Augmented Reasoning for Scalable and Explainable Financial Fraud Detection

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as part of complex agentic systems that orchestrate the use of external tools, such as retrieval mechanisms or code interpreters. In this survey, we argue that this development necessitates a rethinking of the goals of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI): Rather than focusing on providing users with explanations for monolithic machine learning models, we need system-level explanations that also provide information about which and how tools are used, as well as how external execution traces causally influence system behavior. We provide an overview of the existing methods in explainable AI and discuss the limitations of monolithic XAI methods in agentic contexts. Finally, we highlight open challenges in providing faithful explanations for LLM-based systems.</jats:p>
title: From Models to Systems: A Survey of Explainability for Tool-Augmented Language Models and AI Agents
